decks.title: Revenue and Producer's Equilibrium — Part 1: Revenue Concepts and Curves
goals: Calculate total, average and marginal revenue from a schedule
Draw and explain the revenue curves under perfect competition
Draw and explain the revenue curves under imperfect competition and relate TR to MR

slides.heading: Revenue and Producer's Equilibrium
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **total, average and marginal revenue**, and the **revenue curves** of a firm under **perfect** and **imperfect** competition.

nodes.label: Why MR can be below AR

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning of revenue, total, average and marginal revenue, perfect competition curves, why marginal revenue can be below average revenue, imperfect competition curves, and the link between total and marginal revenue
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Costs tell a firm what it pays. Revenue tells it what it receives from selling its output. In this part we meet three measures of revenue, see how a firm that takes the market price differs from one that must cut its price to sell more, and link the shape of total revenue to marginal revenue.

slides.heading: Total, average and marginal revenue

rows: P × Q, or the sum of all MRs
Addition to TR from one more unit

visual.alt: Table of revenue concepts: total revenue is all receipts, found as price times quantity or the sum of marginal revenues; average revenue is revenue per unit, total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price; marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from one more unit

slides.narration: Total revenue is everything a firm receives from selling its output: price times quantity. Average revenue is total revenue per unit sold, and since every unit sells at the price, it is simply the price. Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit, found by subtracting the previous total revenue.

slides.heading: Quick check: what is marginal revenue?
slides.body_md: For a seller of terracotta lamps at an imagined Bishnupur fair, marginal revenue is the…
slides.narration: Ask yourself: is it about all the lamps together, each lamp on average, or just one more lamp?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a kurta workshop's revenue schedule
slides.body_md: An imagined Lucknow chikan workshop must lower its price to sell more kurtas. Work out TR and MR from its prices.
bullets: Step 1 — TR = AR × Q for each output.
Step 2 — MR = TR of this output − TR of the previous output.
Step 3 — Compare MR with AR at each output.

visual.alt: Revenue schedule of an imagined Lucknow chikan workshop: prices 100, 90, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40 for 1 to 7 kurtas give total revenues 100, 180, 240, 280, 300, 300, 280 and marginal revenues 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0, -20
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ hundred.

slides.narration: Multiply each price by the number of kurtas to get total revenue: one hundred, one hundred and eighty, two hundred and forty, and so on. Then subtract each total from the next to find marginal revenue. Notice that marginal revenue falls faster than price, reaches zero at six kurtas and becomes negative at the seventh.

slides.heading: Average revenue is the demand curve
slides.body_md: AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = **P**. Plotting AR against quantity gives the **price** at which each quantity can be sold: the **demand curve** facing the firm.

nodes.label: AR curve = demand curve of the firm

visual.alt: Flow showing that total revenue is price times quantity, so average revenue equals price at every output, and the average revenue curve is the firm's demand curve
visual.caption: Why AR equals price

slides.narration: Because total revenue is price times quantity, dividing by quantity always leaves the price. So average revenue is just another name for price. A curve that shows the price at which each quantity can be sold is the demand curve, which is why the average revenue curve of a firm is also its demand curve.

slides.heading: Quick check: total revenue from marginal revenue
slides.body_md: A dhaba owner in an imagined Karnal highway town records the MR of his 1st, 2nd and 3rd thalis. Find his TR from 3 thalis.
slides.narration: Each marginal revenue is what one thali added. What do you get if you add them all up?

slides.heading: Perfect competition: AR = MR
slides.body_md: A **price taker** sells every unit at the **market price**, so **AR = MR = P**: one **horizontal** line.

slides.narration: Since each coil adds the same forty rupees, total revenue rises in equal steps: forty, eighty, one hundred and twenty. slides.heading: Worked example 2: a price taker's schedule
slides.body_md: An imagined Alappuzha coir-rope maker sells at **₹40** a coil. Build her schedule.
bullets: Step 1 — TR = 40 × Q.
Step 2 — AR = TR ÷ Q = 40.
Step 3 — MR = change in TR = 40.

visual.alt: Revenue schedule of an imagined coir-rope maker selling at 40 rupees: total revenue rises by 40 with each coil, and average and marginal revenue both stay at 40
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹.

slides.narration: Total revenue is forty times the number of coils. Dividing by the number of coils always gives forty, and each extra coil adds forty. So the schedule shows average and marginal revenue fixed at forty, and total revenue climbing by forty each time.

slides.heading: Why MR falls below AR when price must fall
slides.body_md: To sell **one more**, the firm lowers the price on **all** units. MR = price of the extra unit − loss on the earlier units.

visual.alt: Table for an imagined Jaipur blue-pottery studio cutting its price from 500 to 480 rupees to sell a fifth vase: it gains 480 on the extra vase but loses 80 on the first four, so marginal revenue is 400, which matches the rise in total revenue from 2,000 to 2,400
visual.caption: Imagined figures: MR = price of the extra unit − loss on earlier units.

slides.narration: Suppose a pottery studio sells four vases at five hundred rupees and must drop the price to four hundred and eighty to sell a fifth. The fifth vase brings four hundred and eighty, but the first four now earn twenty rupees less each, eighty in all. So marginal revenue is only four hundred, below the price.

slides.heading: Imperfect competition: AR and MR
slides.body_md: Both **slope downward**; **MR lies below AR**. With a straight-line AR, MR starts at the **same point** and falls **twice as steeply**.

slides.heading: Perfect versus imperfect competition
columns: **Perfect competition:** price given; **AR = MR** horizontal; **TR** a straight line; MR never negative.
**Imperfect competition:** price must fall to sell more; **MR < AR**, both falling; **TR** an inverted U; MR can be negative.

rows: Set by the firm; must fall to sell more
Both slope down, MR below AR

visual.alt: Table comparing revenue curves: under perfect competition price is given, average and marginal revenue are one horizontal line and total revenue is a straight line from the origin; under imperfect competition price must fall to sell more, both curves slope down with marginal revenue below, and total revenue is an inverted U that peaks where marginal revenue is zero

slides.narration: Put the two side by side. A price taker faces one flat line for average and marginal revenue and a straight total revenue line. A firm that must cut its price faces falling curves with marginal revenue below average revenue, and its total revenue rises, peaks and falls.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: TR = P × Q; AR = TR ÷ Q = P; MR = TRn − TRn−1
AR = MR horizontal; TR a straight line
AR, MR slope down; MR < AR

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Total revenue is price times quantity, average revenue equals price, and marginal revenue is the change in total revenue. A price taker has flat average and marginal revenue and a straight total revenue line. A firm that must cut its price has marginal revenue below average revenue, and its total revenue peaks where marginal revenue is zero.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **formula** above each column: TR = AR × Q, MR = TRn − TRn−1.
Say **why** AR equals price and why AR is the **demand curve**.
Under perfect competition draw **one** horizontal line labelled **AR = MR**.
With a straight-line AR, MR has the **same intercept** and **twice the slope**.
Link TR to MR: **rising** (MR > 0), **maximum** (MR = 0), **falling** (MR < 0).
slides.narration: Show formulas for every column so method marks are safe. Explain why average revenue is price rather than just stating it. Label the flat line under perfect competition as both average and marginal revenue. Remember the double slope of marginal revenue for a straight demand line, and always tie the shape of total revenue to the sign of marginal revenue.

goals: Find the profit-maximising output by the TR–TC approach from a schedule and a diagram
State and apply the two conditions of the MR–MC approach

slides.heading: Producer's Equilibrium
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the output at which a producer **maximises profit**, by the **TR–TC** and the **MR–MC** approaches.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: profit as total revenue minus total cost, the total revenue and total cost approach, the marginal revenue and marginal cost approach, its two conditions, schedules without exact equality, and why both approaches agree
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: A producer is in equilibrium when it has no reason to change its output, because that output gives the largest profit. There are two ways to find it: by comparing totals, total revenue against total cost, or by comparing margins, the revenue and cost of one more unit. Both lead to the same answer.

slides.heading: Two approaches to the same goal

rows: Biggest vertical gap between TR and TC

visual.alt: Table of the two approaches to producer's equilibrium: by total revenue and total cost, the output with the largest positive gap; by marginal revenue and marginal cost, the output where they are equal and marginal cost is rising
visual.caption: Both give the same output.

slides.narration: Profit is total revenue minus total cost. The first approach looks for the output where this gap is the largest. The second looks at each extra unit: as long as it adds more to revenue than to cost, produce it. The firm stops where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and marginal cost is rising.

slides.heading: The TR–TC approach on a diagram
slides.body_md: Equilibrium is where **TR lies furthest above TC**. Where the curves **cross**, profit is **zero** (break-even).

slides.body_md: An imagined Tiruppur T-shirt unit sells at ₹30 hundred a batch. With its total costs, its largest profit is…
slides.narration: Work out revenue for each output, subtract cost, and look for the biggest figure.

slides.body_md: Find the equilibrium output of an imagined Tiruppur T-shirt unit by the **TR–TC** approach.
bullets: Step 1 — TR = 30 × Q.
Step 2 — Profit = TR − TC for each output.
Step 3 — Pick the largest profit; where two outputs tie, take the one where MR = MC.

slides.narration: Revenue is thirty times the number of batches. Subtracting cost gives profits of minus forty, minus thirty, minus fifteen, five, twenty, twenty and ten. Profit peaks at twenty, at both four and five batches. The fifth batch adds as much to revenue as to cost, so the unit settles at five batches.

slides.heading: The MR–MC approach: two conditions
bullets: **Condition 1: MR = MC.** If MR > MC, produce more; if MR < MC, produce less.
**Condition 2: MC must be rising** at that output (MC cuts MR **from below**), so that beyond it **MC > MR**.

nodes.label: Compare MR and MC for the next unit
MR < MC: do not produce it
Stop where MR = MC with MC rising

visual.alt: Flow of the marginal approach: compare marginal revenue and marginal cost for the next unit; produce it if marginal revenue is larger, not if it is smaller, and stop where they are equal with marginal cost rising
visual.caption: Decide unit by unit

slides.narration: The marginal approach asks one question for each extra unit: does it add more to revenue than to cost? If yes, produce it and profit rises. If no, do not. Profit is greatest where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. But that is not enough: marginal cost must be rising there, so that every unit beyond it would lose money.

slides.heading: MR–MC on a diagram: why MC must be rising
slides.body_md: MC cuts MR **twice**: at **A** (MC falling) and at **B** (MC rising). Only **B** is the equilibrium.

slides.narration: Here marginal revenue is flat at the price of thirty. The U-shaped marginal cost cuts it twice. At A, marginal cost is still falling, so the next pumps cost less than they earn: producing more adds profit. At B, marginal cost is rising, and every further pump costs more than it earns. So B, at nine pumps, is the equilibrium.

slides.body_md: An imagined Bareilly furniture maker finds MR = MC at an output where MC is still falling. If he stops there…
slides.narration: What happens to marginal cost for the next few units, compared with marginal revenue?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: when MR never exactly equals MC
slides.body_md: An imagined Lucknow chikan workshop: find the equilibrium by the **MR–MC** approach.
bullets: Step 1 — MR = TRn − TRn−1; MC = TCn − TCn−1.
Step 2 — Produce every kurta with MR ≥ MC.
Step 3 — Stop before the first kurta with MR < MC (MC rising).

visual.alt: Marginal revenue and marginal cost of an imagined Lucknow chikan workshop for 1 to 6 kurtas: marginal revenue 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0 against marginal cost 60, 50, 40, 50, 70, 90; marginal revenue is at least marginal cost only up to the third kurta
visual.caption: Equilibrium: 3 kurtas, profit 40 (₹ hundred).

slides.narration: Here no output has marginal revenue exactly equal to marginal cost. So produce each kurta that adds at least as much to revenue as to cost. The first three do: sixty against forty for the third. The fourth adds forty to revenue but fifty to cost. So the workshop stops at three kurtas, where profit is forty, the most in the schedule.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: two points where MR = MC
slides.body_md: An imagined Jodhpur leather-bag unit sells at **₹25**. Where is it in equilibrium?
bullets: Step 1 — MR = 25 for every bag.
Step 2 — MR = MC at the 1st bag and the 5th bag.
Step 3 — Reject the 1st bag (MC falling); accept the 5th (MC rising).

visual.alt: Schedule of an imagined Jodhpur leather-bag unit selling at 25 with a fixed cost of 10: marginal cost 25, 18, 15, 20, 25, 32; marginal revenue equals marginal cost at the first bag, where marginal cost is falling, and at the fifth bag, where it is rising; profit is highest at the fifth bag
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹.

slides.narration: Marginal revenue is twenty-five for every bag. The first bag costs exactly twenty-five, but then the cost of extra bags falls, so producing more adds profit. The fifth bag also costs twenty-five, and after it the cost jumps to thirty-two. Profit is highest, twelve rupees, at five bags, which confirms the second condition.

slides.heading: Quick check: equilibrium of the bag unit
slides.body_md: From the bag unit's price of ₹25 and its marginal costs, find its equilibrium output.
slides.narration: Find both outputs where marginal cost equals twenty-five, then check which way marginal cost is moving.

slides.heading: Why both approaches give the same output
slides.body_md: The slope of TR is **MR** and the slope of TC is **MC**. The gap TR − TC is largest where the two curves are **parallel**: **MR = MC**.

rows: TR is steeper than TC (MR > MC)
TR and TC are parallel (MR = MC)
TC is steeper than TR (MC > MR)

visual.alt: Table linking the two approaches: the gap between total revenue and total cost widens while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, is largest where the two curves are parallel and marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and narrows once marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue

slides.narration: Look again at the total diagram. While total revenue is steeper than total cost, the gap between them widens: marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost. Once total cost becomes steeper, the gap narrows. The widest gap is where the two curves have the same slope, which is exactly where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

slides.heading: Equilibrium under perfect and imperfect competition
slides.body_md: Under perfect competition **MR = P**, so the condition becomes **MC = P** with MC rising.

visual.alt: Table showing that under perfect competition marginal revenue equals price, so equilibrium is where marginal cost equals price with marginal cost rising; under imperfect competition marginal revenue is below price, so marginal cost equals marginal revenue at an output where price is higher

slides.narration: The rule is the same for every firm, but it looks different. A price taker's marginal revenue is the price, so it produces where marginal cost equals the price and is rising. A firm that must cut its price has marginal revenue below the price, so at its equilibrium the price is higher than marginal cost.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Produce up to the last unit with MR ≥ MC
Same output: slopes of TR and TC equal

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the two approaches to producer's equilibrium, what to do when a schedule has no exact equality, and why both approaches agree

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. By the total approach, the producer chooses the output with the largest positive gap between total revenue and total cost. By the marginal approach, it produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost with marginal cost rising, or up to the last unit where marginal revenue is at least marginal cost. Both give the same output.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always state **both** conditions: MR = MC **and** MC rising (cutting MR from below).
In schedules, add **TR, profit, MR and MC** columns with formulas.
If two outputs tie for the largest profit, choose the one where **MR = MC**.
If no MR equals MC exactly, produce up to the last unit with **MR ≥ MC**.
On diagrams, mark the **equilibrium output** on the x-axis and label every curve.
slides.narration: Examiners look for both conditions, so never stop at marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Show your columns with formulas. When two outputs give the same profit, explain why the larger one is chosen. When no exact equality appears, stop at the last unit worth producing. And on diagrams, label the curves and mark the equilibrium output.

notes.title: Revenue and Producer's Equilibrium — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Total, average and marginal revenue
sections.body_md:
- **Total revenue (TR)** = P × Q; also the sum of the MRs of all units sold.
- **Average revenue (AR)** = TR ÷ Q = **P**. The AR curve is the firm's **demand curve**.
- **Marginal revenue (MR)** = TRn − TRn−1: the addition to TR from selling one more unit.
- If TR falls when one more unit is sold, MR is **negative**.

key_terms.definition_md: Revenue per unit sold; always equal to the price.
The change in total revenue from selling one more unit.

rows: P × Q, or the sum of all MRs
Addition to TR from one more unit

visual.alt: Table of revenue concepts: total revenue is all receipts, found as price times quantity or the sum of marginal revenues; average revenue is revenue per unit, total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price; marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from one more unit

sections.heading: 2. Revenue curves under perfect competition
sections.body_md:
A firm under perfect competition is a **price taker**: it sells any quantity at the market price, and asking more would lose all its buyers (perfectly elastic demand).

- **AR = MR = P**: one **horizontal** line.
- **TR**: a **straight line from the origin** with slope P; it has no maximum.

key_terms.definition_md: A firm too small to affect the market price, which it accepts as given.

sections.heading: 3. Revenue curves under imperfect competition
sections.body_md:
Under monopoly and monopolistic competition the firm must **lower its price** to sell more, so **AR slopes downward** (more elastic under monopolistic competition, where close substitutes exist).

- MR = price of the extra unit − loss on the earlier units, so **MR < AR**.
- With a straight-line AR = a − bQ: TR = aQ − bQ² and **MR = a − 2bQ**: same intercept, **twice the slope**.
- **TR** rises while MR > 0, is **maximum where MR = 0**, and falls when MR < 0: an **inverted U**.

key_terms.definition_md: The total revenue curve of a firm that must cut its price to sell more: it rises, peaks where MR = 0, then falls.

sections.heading: 4. Producer's equilibrium: the TR–TC approach
sections.body_md:
Profit = TR − TC. The producer is in equilibrium at the output where this **positive gap is the largest**.

- On a diagram, TC starts at **TFC** above the origin; TR (perfect competition) starts at the origin.
- Where TR and TC **cross**, profit is zero: **break-even** points.
- At the largest gap the **slopes** of TR and TC are equal.

key_terms.definition_md: The output at which a producer earns the maximum profit and has no reason to change output.
An output where TR = TC and profit is zero.

sections.heading: 5. Producer's equilibrium: the MR–MC approach
sections.body_md:
**Conditions:** (1) **MR = MC**; (2) **MC is rising** at that output, i.e. MC cuts MR **from below**, so beyond it MC > MR.

- If MR > MC, more output raises profit; if MR < MC, less output raises profit.
- An MR = MC point with **MC falling** is **not** an equilibrium (profit is lowest there).
- Perfect competition: MR = P, so equilibrium is where **MC = P** and MC is rising.

key_terms.definition_md: At equilibrium MC must be rising, cutting MR from below.

sections.body_md:
- Build **TR, profit, MR and MC** columns, each with its formula.
- If **no output has MR exactly equal to MC**, produce every unit with **MR ≥ MC** and stop before the first unit with MR < MC.
- If MR = MC exactly at an output, profit is the **same** at that output and the one before it; the equilibrium is the output where **MR = MC**.
- Both approaches agree: the slope of TR is MR, the slope of TC is MC, and the gap TR − TC is widest where the slopes are equal.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying AR equals MR for every firm: only under perfect competition.
- Drawing MR above AR, or MR with the same slope as a straight-line AR.
- Choosing the output of maximum TR (MR = 0) as the profit-maximising output.
- Stating only MR = MC and forgetting that MC must be rising.
- Computing MR as TR ÷ Q, or subtracting the next total instead of the previous one.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, value or term.
- 2 marks: a definition with an example, or a value with working.
- 3 marks: three linked points, or a completed short schedule.
- 5 marks: parts answered in order, with schedules or described diagrams and reasons.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Varanasi silk-saree weaver earns ₹48,000 by selling 6 sarees at one price. Her average revenue per saree is ₹8,000, which is the same as

options.text_md: her marginal revenue in every case
her total revenue divided by her total cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the price of a saree. AR = TR ÷ Q = 48,000 ÷ 6 = 8,000. When every unit sells at the same price, revenue per unit is that price, so AR always equals price. MR need not equal AR, and profit per unit needs cost too.

options.text_md: total revenue divided by the number of lamps sold
price of the last lamp minus its cost
revenue earned from the first lamp only
change in total revenue from selling one more lamp

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** change in total revenue from selling one more lamp. MR = TRn − TRn−1, the addition to total revenue from one more unit sold. TR ÷ Q is average revenue; price minus cost is a profit idea.

questions.stem_md: A dhaba owner in an imagined Karnal highway town records the marginal revenue of his 1st, 2nd and 3rd thalis as ₹120, ₹110 and ₹100. His total revenue from 3 thalis is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹330. TR is the sum of the marginal revenues of all units sold: 120 + 110 + 100 = 330.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** negative. MR is the change in TR. If TR falls when one more unit is sold, the change is negative, so MR is negative.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹60 hundred. Price = AR = TR ÷ Q = 300 ÷ 5 = 60. The MR of the 5th kurta is 20, a different idea.

questions.stem_md: Define total revenue and marginal revenue, using an imagined Puri seashell-craft stall as your example.
questions.solution_md: One definition with an example for each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Total revenue** is the **whole amount received** from sales: if the stall sells 20 shell boxes at ₹50, TR is ₹1,000. **Marginal revenue** is the **addition to TR from selling one more box**, for example the change when the 21st box is sold.

questions.stem_md: Show why average revenue is always equal to price, taking an imagined Shimla apple grower who sells Q boxes at a price P each.
questions.solution_md: Algebraic link TR = P × Q, then divide by Q.

answer.model_answer_md: Total revenue is **TR = P × Q**. Average revenue is **TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P**. So whatever the number of boxes, **revenue per box equals the price** at which they are sold.

questions.stem_md:
The prices at which an imagined Lucknow chikan workshop can sell its kurtas are shown below. Calculate total revenue and marginal revenue for 1 to 4 kurtas.

| Kurtas | AR (₹ hundred) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 100 |
| 2 | 90 |
| 3 | 80 |
| 4 | 70 |
questions.solution_md: TR from AR × Q, then MR from differences.

answer.model_answer_md:
**TR = AR × Q:** 100 × 1 = **100**; 90 × 2 = **180**; 80 × 3 = **240**; 70 × 4 = **280**.
**MR = TRn − TRn−1:** **100**, **80**, **60**, **40**. MR falls faster than AR because a lower price must be accepted on every kurta to sell one more.

marking_scheme.step: Correct working or remark on MR below AR

questions.stem_md: An imagined Kanpur leather-belt seller notices that his total revenue keeps rising but by smaller amounts each day he cuts prices. Explain what is happening to his marginal revenue at each stage as TR rises, stops rising and then falls.
questions.solution_md: MR is the slope of TR: positive, zero, negative.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. While **TR rises**, each extra belt adds something, so **MR is positive** (and here falling).
2. Where **TR is at its maximum**, the last belt adds nothing, so **MR = 0**.
3. If he cuts the price further and **TR falls**, the extra belt reduces revenue, so **MR is negative**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Alappuzha coir-rope maker can sell any number of coils at the market price of ₹40. Her AR and MR curves are

options.text_md: two downward-sloping lines, MR below AR
a single upward-sloping line through the origin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the same horizontal line at ₹40. Price is fixed by the market, so every extra coil adds ₹40 (MR = 40) and revenue per coil is ₹40 (AR = 40): one horizontal line. A straight line through the origin is her TR curve.

questions.stem_md: For a price-taking wheat farmer in an imagined Hoshiarpur village, the total revenue curve is

options.text_md: a horizontal line at the market price
an upward-sloping straight line starting from the origin

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an upward-sloping straight line starting from the origin. With a constant price, TR = P × Q rises by the same amount for each unit, so TR is a straight line through the origin with slope equal to the price.

questions.stem_md: Why does one of thousands of identical potato growers in an imagined Hooghly district face a horizontal average revenue curve?

options.text_md: It can raise its price without losing any buyers
Its output is too small to change the market price, so it sells every unit at that price
It has to lower its price to sell every extra unit
The government fixes a different price for each grower

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Its output is too small to change the market price, so it sells every unit at that price. Each grower is a price taker: its supply is a tiny share of the market, so the industry fixes the price and the grower sells all it wants at that price. Raising the price would lose all buyers.

questions.stem_md: The total revenue line of an imagined Alappuzha coir-rope maker passes through (0, 0) and (5 coils, ₹200). The market price of a coil must be
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹40. The slope of the TR line is the price: 200 ÷ 5 = 40.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under perfect competition, the marginal revenue of a firm equals its average revenue at every output.

**Reason (R):** Every extra unit is sold at the same market price, so it adds exactly that price to total revenue.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: with a constant price, the addition to TR from each unit is the price (MR = P), and revenue per unit is also the price (AR = P).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A perfectly competitive bangle seller in an imagined Firozabad market will find that her total revenue reaches a maximum and then falls as she sells more.
questions.solution_md: **False.** With a constant price, TR rises by the same amount for every extra unit, so it keeps rising in a straight line; it has no maximum. TR falls only when the price must be cut to sell more.

questions.stem_md: Describe the TR, AR and MR curves of an imagined Hooghly potato grower who sells at a market price of ₹15 a kg.
questions.solution_md: AR = MR horizontal; TR a ray from the origin.

answer.model_answer_md: **AR and MR** are the **same horizontal line** at ₹15, because each kilogram fetches and adds ₹15. **TR** is a **straight line from the origin** rising by ₹15 for each extra kilogram.

marking_scheme.step: AR = MR horizontal at the price
TR straight line from the origin

questions.stem_md: Explain why an imagined Alappuzha coir-rope maker who tried to sell above the market price of ₹40 would sell nothing at all.
questions.solution_md: Homogeneous product and many sellers make demand perfectly elastic.

answer.model_answer_md: Thousands of sellers offer **identical** coils at ₹40 and buyers have **full knowledge** of prices. If she asks more, buyers simply **switch to other sellers**, so her sales fall to **zero**: her demand is **perfectly elastic** at ₹40.

marking_scheme.step: Identical product, many sellers, full knowledge

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Alappuzha coir-rope maker sells at the market price shown. Prepare her TR, AR and MR schedule for 1 to 5 coils and state the shape of each curve.

| Coils sold | Price (₹) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 40 |
| 2 | 40 |
| 3 | 40 |
| 4 | 40 |
| 5 | 40 |
questions.solution_md: Constant price gives constant AR and MR and a linear TR.

answer.model_answer_md: **TR:** 40, 80, 120, 160, 200; **AR:** 40, 40, 40, 40, 40; **MR:** 40, 40, 40, 40, 40. AR and MR form **one horizontal line at ₹40**, because she is a price taker and every coil both fetches and adds the same ₹40. questions.stem_md:
Compare the revenue curves of (i) an imagined Hooghly potato grower selling at a market price and (ii) an imagined Lucknow chikan workshop that must lower its price to sell more kurtas.

(a) Describe the AR and MR curves of each firm and give the reason. [3]
(b) Describe the TR curve of each firm. [2]
questions.solution_md: Horizontal AR = MR versus downward AR with MR below; linear TR versus inverted-U TR.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) The potato grower is a **price taker**: AR = MR = price, a **single horizontal line**, because each kilogram adds the same price. (ii) The workshop faces a **downward-sloping AR** (its demand curve). To sell one more kurta it must cut the price on **all** kurtas, so **MR < AR** and the MR curve lies **below** AR (and falls twice as steeply when AR is a straight line).
(b) (i) The grower's **TR is a straight line from the origin**, rising by the price for each unit. (ii) The workshop's **TR rises at a decreasing rate**, reaches a **maximum where MR = 0**, and then **falls** when MR becomes negative.

marking_scheme.step: Imperfect: AR slopes down, MR below
Reason: price cut on all units
TR rises, peaks at MR = 0, falls

questions.stem_md: An imagined Jaipur blue-pottery studio must lower the price of all its vases to sell one more. As a result its marginal revenue is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** less than its average revenue. The extra vase brings in its price, but the price cut on all the earlier vases is a loss, so the addition to TR (MR) is less than the price (AR).

questions.stem_md: The total revenue of an imagined Kanchipuram silk seller is at its highest. At this output her marginal revenue is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** zero. TR stops rising where an extra unit adds nothing, that is, where MR = 0. Beyond it MR is negative and TR falls.

questions.stem_md: A monopoly water-tanker supplier in an imagined hill town faces a straight-line AR curve. Its MR curve starts from the same point on the price axis and

options.text_md: falls half as steeply as AR
falls twice as steeply as AR

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** falls twice as steeply as AR. With a straight-line AR = a − bQ, TR = aQ − bQ², so MR = a − 2bQ: same intercept, twice the slope. MR cuts the quantity axis halfway to where AR does.

questions.stem_md: At what output does the marginal revenue of the imagined Lucknow chikan workshop first become negative, given its prices of ₹100, 90, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40 hundred for 1 to 7 kurtas?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 7 kurtas. TR: 100, 180, 240, 280, 300, 300, 280. MR: 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0, -20. The first negative MR (-20) is at the 7th kurta.

questions.stem_md: Many cafés in an imagined Pune college area sell slightly different cold coffees. The AR curve of one café is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** downward-sloping and fairly elastic. Each café's product is a little different, so it can raise its price and keep some buyers (AR slopes down), but close substitutes make demand fairly elastic.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve can have a negative marginal revenue.

**Reason (R):** Average revenue is always positive because the price of a good cannot be negative.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. MR becomes negative when the loss from cutting the price on earlier units exceeds the price of the extra unit; that average revenue stays positive is true but does not explain why MR turns negative.

questions.stem_md: When a firm's total revenue is at its maximum, its marginal revenue is ___.
questions.solution_md: TR is highest where MR = zero.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Lucknow chikan workshop can sell 1 to 7 kurtas at prices of ₹100, 90, 80, 70, 60, 50, 40 hundred. Find the output at which its marginal revenue is zero.
Using an imagined Jaipur blue-pottery studio that cuts its vase price from ₹500 to ₹480 to sell a 5th vase, explain why marginal revenue is less than price.
questions.solution_md: Gain from the extra unit minus loss on earlier units.

answer.model_answer_md: The 5th vase brings in **₹480**, but the price falls by ₹20 on the **4 earlier vases**, a loss of **₹80**. So MR = 480 − 80 = **₹400**, less than the price of ₹480. TR goes from 2,000 to 2,400.

questions.stem_md: Describe the AR and MR curves of a sole cable-TV operator in an imagined small town who must lower his monthly fee to gain more subscribers.
questions.solution_md: Downward-sloping AR and MR, with MR below AR.

answer.model_answer_md: Both curves **slope downward**: to gain subscribers he must **lower the fee**. **MR lies below AR** because the lower fee applies to **all** subscribers, so the extra revenue is less than the fee.

marking_scheme.step: MR below AR, with the reason

questions.stem_md: Explain the shape of the total revenue curve of an imagined Kanchipuram silk seller who must lower her price to sell more sarees, relating each part to marginal revenue.
questions.solution_md: Three stages of TR matched with MR.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. At first TR **rises at a decreasing rate**, because **MR is positive but falling**.
2. TR reaches its **highest point** where **MR = 0**.
3. After that TR **falls**, because **MR is negative**. So the curve is an **inverted U**.

marking_scheme.step: Rising at a decreasing rate: MR positive, falling

questions.stem_md: An imagined hill-town water-tanker monopolist faces AR = 12 − Q (price in ₹ hundred, Q in tankers a day). Write its TR and MR, and find the output at which TR is greatest.
questions.solution_md: TR from AR × Q; MR halves the quantity intercept; MR = 0 at Q = 6.

answer.model_answer_md: **TR = AR × Q = 12Q − Q²**. MR is the change in TR: **MR = 12 − 2Q** (same intercept, twice the slope of AR). TR is greatest where **MR = 0**, at **Q = 6** tankers, where TR = 36.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined hill-town water-tanker monopolist faces AR = 12 − Q (₹ hundred).

(a) Calculate AR, TR and MR at Q = 2, 6 and 8. [3]
(b) Use the figures to explain why MR lies below AR and how TR behaves. [2]
questions.solution_md: Values from the equations, then the reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Q = 2:** AR = 10, TR = 20, MR = 8. **Q = 6:** AR = 6, TR = 36, MR = 0. **Q = 8:** AR = 4, TR = 32, MR = -4. (TR = 12Q − Q², MR = 12 − 2Q.)
(b) At every output **MR < AR** (8 < 10, 0 < 6), because the price must be cut on **all** tankers to sell one more. TR **rises** while MR is positive, **peaks at 36 when MR = 0** (Q = 6), and **falls** to 32 when MR turns negative.

marking_scheme.step: TR rises, peaks at MR = 0, falls

questions.stem_md: By the TR–TC approach, an imagined Bhagalpur silk-yarn unit is in equilibrium at the output where

options.text_md: total revenue is at its maximum
the positive gap between total revenue and total cost is the largest
total cost is at its minimum

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the positive gap between total revenue and total cost is the largest. Profit = TR − TC, so the profit-maximising output is where TR exceeds TC by the most. TR = TC is the break-even point, with zero profit.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Tiruppur T-shirt unit sells at ₹30 hundred a batch. With its total costs of ₹40, 60, 75, 85, 100, 130, 170 hundred for 0 to 6 batches, its largest profit is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹20 hundred. Profit = 30Q − TC: -40, -30, -15, 5, 20, 20, 10. The largest is 20 (at 4 and 5 batches).

questions.stem_md: On the TR–TC diagram of an imagined Kota coaching-notes printer, the points where the TR and TC curves cross show

options.text_md: the output of maximum total revenue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** break-even outputs with zero profit. Where TR = TC, profit is zero: these are break-even points. Profit is greatest where TR lies furthest above TC.

questions.stem_md: At the output where the gap between TR and TC is greatest for an imagined Rajkot engineering firm, the slopes of the two curves are

options.text_md: such that TR is steeper, so MR is greater than MC
such that TC is steeper, so MC is greater than MR

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** equal, so MR equals MC. The vertical gap stops widening where the curves are parallel. The slope of TR is MR and the slope of TC is MC, so at the largest gap MR = MC: both approaches give the same output.

**Assertion (A):** A firm does not necessarily maximise profit at the output where its total revenue is the highest.

**Reason (R):** Profit depends on total cost as well as total revenue, and costs keep rising with output.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: at the TR maximum the extra cost of the last units still has to be paid, so the largest TR − TC gap usually lies at a smaller output.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Tiruppur T-shirt unit sells 5 batches at ₹30 hundred a batch and its total cost is ₹130 hundred. Find its profit (in ₹ hundred).

answer.model_answer_md:

Drop a line from **B** to the x-axis to show the **equilibrium output**.
(b) At **A**, MC is falling, so for the units just after A **MC < MR** and producing them **adds profit**: A is not an equilibrium. At **B**, MC is rising, so beyond B **MC > MR** and more output **cuts profit**; both conditions hold, so **B** is the equilibrium.

questions.solution_md: Perfect competition schedule and curves; imperfect competition schedule and TR shape.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **TR:** 40, 80, 120, 160; **AR = MR = 40** at every output. She is one of many sellers of an identical product, so she accepts the market price and can sell any quantity at it. AR and MR therefore form **one horizontal line** at ₹40. TR is a **straight line from the origin** with slope 40, because each coil adds the same price; it has no maximum.
(ii) **TR:** 100, 180, 240, 280, 300, 300, 280; **MR:** 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0, -20. TR **rises at a decreasing rate** while MR is positive and falling, **peaks at 300** where **MR = 0** (6 kurtas), and **falls** when MR turns **negative** at the 7th kurta: an **inverted U**. The workshop must lower the price on all kurtas to sell one more, which is why MR lies below AR and keeps falling.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **MR:** 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0; **MC:** 60, 50, 40, 50, 70, 90. MR exceeds MC up to the **3rd kurta** (60 > 40) and falls below it at the 4th (40 < 50), with MC **rising**, so equilibrium is **3 kurtas**. Profit = 240 − 200 = **40** (₹ hundred), the highest in the schedule.

While **TR is steeper than TC** (MR > MC), the gap **widens**; once **TC is steeper** (MC > MR), it **narrows**. The gap is greatest where the **slopes are equal**, where a tangent to TC is **parallel** to the tangent to TR, that is where **MR = MC** with MC rising. So both approaches give the same output.
